segments.text: Hey guys, welcome to this deep dive on
AWS Cloud Trail. Cloud Trail records API
calls made in our AWS accounts by users,
services, and applications. It logs
details such as who made the request,
what action was taken, which resources
were touched, and when it happened. You
can then send logs to S3, Cloudatch
logs, or Event Bridge for monitoring and
alerting. and it helps with security
audits, troubleshooting, compliance, and
tracking changes across your AWS
environment. API auditing with Cloud
Trail records information including
which user or service made a request for
an action, which of course is an API
call, on which resources, and at what
date and time. Here's an example. So,
here's the summary information of an
event. You can see who made the request,
when it was made. So we got the event
time, we got the username, the actual
event, this was the run instances API
action. That's an EC2 related API call.
We can see the access key that was used,
the source IP address and so on. If I go
across to AWS here, in fact, I've also
run that particular action very
recently. So if I go to event history,
we can see here I've actually searched
for it. But if I if I pull that out,
then we can choose information in the
lookup attributes here. So for example,
what I did then is I searched for the

trail we need to create something called

there automatically. So every account in
AWS is going to have that information

trail logs any events to S3 or cloudatch

logging API actions sending that

Athena could then be used to query cloud
trail using SQL. So querying the cloud
trail logs in S3. Alternatively, we
could send that information to cloudatch
logs. So we can store information in

via subscription filters to trigger
based on certain events that happen. You
can also trigger lambda of course and
SNS. Now another way of doing this would
be to use event bridge event buses
directly to respond to events that

that have happened and trigger a lambda

important to note that you do need to

you do need a trail for that. So in this
case, API events trigger lambda
functions or an SNS topic. Now there are
different event types within AWS cloud
trail. There are management events.
These are control plane actions. So
creating, updating or deleting AWS
resources. There are data events which
are data plane actions inside resources.
There are insights events which detect
unusual API activity like spikes in
calls or abnormal error rates. And there
are network activity events which are
API calls and service calls in that
traverse a VPC endpoint. So management
events record control plane actions
meaning operations that actually change
the configuration of the resource
itself. Examples here would be creating
a VPC, updating a security group,
deleting an S3 bucket, and starting or
stopping an EC2 instance. They're
enabled by default in cloud trial
because they track important account
level changes. Here's an example
management event. So you can see this
one is an EC2 event which is starting an
EC2 instance. Then we got the data
event. So these record data plane
actions meaning activity inside a
resource. Examples here would be S3
object level actions like get object or
put object or delete object, Lambda
function invocations and Dynamob item
level operations. They're not enabled by
default because they do generate a very
large amount of log information. So
that's just something to bear in mind.
Here's an example data event. This is an
S3 related one where we're trying to get
the objects within an S3 bucket. Then we
got the insights events. These detect
unusual or unexpected API activity in
your AWS account. They show spikes,
drops, or abnormal patterns compared to
your normal baseline. And they help you
to identify issues like
misconfigurations, automation loops, or
potential security problems. Insights
events provide a summary record plus a
detailed insight event showing what
changed and when. And here's an example
of an insights event. So here we can see
it's using some averages. So we've got a
baseline and then we got an insight
amount for certain events. In this case
describing EC2 instances. Lastly, we
have the network activity events. So
these are the ones that capture requests
made through VPC endpoints or supported
network paths. They log which account or
service made the network call, the
target service and whether it was then
allowed or denied. It helps to verify
access patterns for private connectivity
setups like private link. Very useful
for debugging endpoint policies, block
requests, and unexpected network usage.
And here's an example network activity
event. We can see uh this one is
actually associated with a particular
VPC endpoint ID. We got a username and
then we got the request parameters that
were sent as part of that request.
Another couple of features of AWS cloudt
trail are the cloud trail lake and event
data stores. Cloud trail lake is a
feature that lets you ingest, store and
query cloud trail events using SQL gives
you long-term centralized storage for
audit and security data and you can run
SQL queries directly inside cloud trail
without exporting your log files where
for example you would use AENA. It
supports cloud trail events plus outside
resources like security tool data, apps
or audit logs. Event data stores are
storage containers inside Cloud Trail
Lake where your event data is actually
kept and each store has its own
retention period, access rules, and data
sources. You can create multiple stores
for different teams or compliance needs.
This is used for long-term audit
history, investigations, and advanced
analytics. Cloud Trail Lake also comes
with a dashboard. Lake dashboards show
charts and summaries of your Cloud Trail
Lake data. They can highlight trends
like API usage, errors, and unusual
activity. And it's powered again by SQL
queries that update automatically. Used
for quick audit and security insights.
Cloud trails let you bring external
audit logs into Cloud Trail Lake. They
define how outside systems send events
to AWS. Imported events follow the cloud
trail format and can then be queried. So
this is used to centralize AWS and
nonAWWS activity logs in one place. Now
it's important to understand how you can
deploy cloud trail across multiple
accounts and regions because often we do
want to make sure that this data is
centralized and retained for a long
period of time so we know exactly what's
happening across all of our AWS accounts
and regions. So here is one way of doing
it. We've got account A and account B
with cloud trail running and then we got
account C with an S3 bucket and
essentially we're just forwarding this
information and storing it in the S3
bucket in account C. A bucket policy is
then required for cross account
permissions in account A and account B.
We of course configure the logging to
send data to the S3 bucket and account
C. Another way is using organization
trails. So if all of our accounts are
within an AWS organization, we can
enable an organization trail in the
management account and apply it to
member accounts. Settings can also be
enforced. So accounts cannot turn off
logging even if you're an administrator
in the production or the development
account. We can centrally restrict the
ability to switch off cloud trail. So no
one can override those settings. We want
to make sure that we get this data
centralized into our management account.
logs are centralized into one S3 bucket
in the management account.
